title: Data Types
summary: C's integer, floating-point, character and boolean types: their sizes, limits, printf format specifiers, conversions, and the traps of integer division and signed/unsigned mixing.
introduction: Every value in C has a type, and the type decides how many bytes it uses, which values it can hold and what arithmetic on it means. Unlike dynamic languages, C never guesses: 7 / 2 is 3 because both operands are integers, and an unsigned counter that drops below zero wraps around to a huge number. This lesson tours the built-in types, shows how to print each one, and explains the conversion rules behind most beginner surprises.
learningObjectives: Choose between int, long, unsigned and fixed-width integer types
Explain why floating-point values are approximate and format them with printf
Treat char and bool as the small integers they are
Predict the result of integer division, casts and mixed signed/unsigned arithmetic

blocks.text: C offers several integer types that differ in size, and the standard fixes only minimum ranges: `char` is at least 8 bits, `short` and `int` at least 16, `long` at least 32 and `long long` at least 64. On the 64-bit Linux and macOS systems most people use, `int` is 4 bytes and `long` is 8; on 64-bit Windows `long` is only 4 bytes. Each type has an `unsigned` variant that gives up negative numbers to double the positive range. The `sizeof` operator reports a size in bytes, and `<limits.h>` names the limits of every type.

blocks.title: sizes.c
Terminal (x86-64 Linux; long is 4 bytes on Windows)
blocks.content:
char      1 byte(s)
short     2 byte(s)
int       4 byte(s)
long      8 byte(s)
long long 8 byte(s)
INT_MAX   2147483647
UINT_MAX  4294967295

blocks.text: When the exact size matters, for example in file formats or network protocols, use the fixed-width types from `<stdint.h>`: `int8_t`, `uint8_t`, `int32_t`, `uint64_t` and friends. `size_t` is the unsigned type that `sizeof` produces and that can hold any array index; print it with `%zu`. Each type needs the matching `printf` conversion, and the compiler's `-Wall` warnings tell you when they disagree.

rows: pointer (an address; the value varies per run)

blocks.text: `float` (usually 32 bits, about 7 significant digits) and `double` (64 bits, about 15 to 16 digits) store binary approximations of real numbers. Many decimal fractions, 0.1 among them, have no exact binary representation, so arithmetic accumulates tiny errors. Use `double` by default; `float` only pays off in large arrays. Never compare floating-point results with `==`; compare the difference against a small tolerance instead.

blocks.title: floating.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 floating.c -o floating -lm
$ ./floating
0.3
0.30000000000000004
equal: 0
close: 1
float  0.3333333433
double 0.3333333333

blocks.text: The `-lm` flag links the maths library, which some Linux systems need for `<math.h>` functions such as `fabs`, `sqrt` and `pow`. The literal `1.0f` is a `float`; without the suffix every decimal literal is a `double`.

`char` is a one-byte integer type that usually holds a character code. The literal `'A'` is simply the number 65 in ASCII, so arithmetic works on it: `'A' + 1` is 66, which prints as `B`. Whether plain `char` is signed or unsigned depends on the platform, so use `unsigned char` when you treat bytes as numbers from 0 to 255. The boolean type `_Bool` is spelled `bool` after `#include <stdbool.h>`, with the constants `true` and `false`; in C23 `bool`, `true` and `false` are keywords and the header is no longer required.

blocks.title: chars.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
A is 65
next: B
lower: a
big = 1
sizeof(bool) = 1

blocks.text: When an expression mixes types, C converts the operands to a common type before computing. Two rules cause most surprises. First, an operation on two integers is an integer operation: `7 / 2` is 3, and the remainder is available separately as `7 % 2`. Second, when a signed value meets an unsigned value of the same size, the signed one is converted to unsigned. A **cast**, written `(type)value`, converts explicitly, and the standard way to get a fractional result from two integers is to cast one operand *before* dividing. Converting a `double` to an integer truncates towards zero; it does not round.

blocks.title: convert.c

blocks.text: Unsigned arithmetic wraps around by definition, which is well defined and occasionally useful. Signed overflow, such as adding 1 to `INT_MAX`, is **undefined behaviour**: the compiler may assume it never happens and optimise accordingly. The [common bugs](/tutorials/c/common-bugs) lesson shows how to check for it safely.

blocks.title: Common mistake: comparing signed with unsigned
blocks.text: In `if (n < limit)` where `n` is `int` and `limit` is `unsigned int`, a negative `n` is converted to unsigned first, so `-1` becomes 4294967295 and the comparison is false. Loops written as `for (int i = 0; i < strlen(s) - 1; i++)` fail the same way when the string is empty. `-Wextra` enables `-Wsign-compare`, which flags every such comparison; the fix is to make both sides the same type.

blocks.title: signed.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 signed.c -o signed
signed.c: In function 'main':
signed.c:8:11: warning: comparison of integer expressions of different signedness: 'int' and 'unsigned int' [-Wsign-compare]
    8 |     if (n < limit)
      |           ^
$ ./signed
n is NOT smaller: it became 4294967295

questions.question: What does this statement print?
questions.explanation: `9 / 4` is integer division and gives 2; multiplying by 2 gives 4. The fraction is lost before the multiplication.

questions.question: Which header provides the fixed-width types `int32_t` and `uint8_t`?
questions.explanation: `<stdint.h>` defines the exact-width integer types. `<limits.h>` holds limits such as `INT_MAX`, and `<stdbool.h>` defines `bool`.
